note: Cards where the English covers visibly more or less text than the Latin recorded beside it (verse division or grouped cards). Reported by the readers; not rewritten.

spans.latin: Pater noster mortuus est in deserto, nec fuit in seditione, quæ concitata est contra Dominum sub Core, sed in peccato suo mortuus est : hic non habuit mares filios. Cur tollitur nomen illius de familia sua, quia non habuit filium ? date nobis possessionem inter cognatos patris nostri.
spans.english: Our father died in the wilderness. He was not part of the rebellion stirred up against the Lord under Korah, but died in his own sin. He had no sons. Why should his name be removed from his family because he had no son? Give us a possession among our father's kinsmen. Moses brought their case before the Lord's judgment. He said to him: The daughters of Zelophehad ask what is just. Give them a possession among their father's kinsmen, and let them succeed him in his inheritance. Speak these things to the children of Israel: When a man dies without a son, his inheritance shall pass to his daughter.
spans.reason: Latin shown is Vg 27:3 only (ends "inter cognatos patris nostri"); English runs on through Vg 27:4-8 ("Moses brought their case ... shall pass to his daughter"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.latin: per agnos decimam decimæ, qui simul sunt agni septem. Hircum quoque,
spans.english: and a tenth of a tenth for each of the seven lambs. Also a male goat shall be slaughtered for atonement, besides the continual burnt offering and its drink offerings. You shall offer everything unblemished, with its drink offerings.
spans.reason: Latin shown stops at "Hircum quoque," (Vg 28:29); English continues through Vg 28:30-31 ("shall be slaughtered for atonement ... with its drink offerings"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.latin: De ipsis autem urbibus, quæ ad fugitivorum subsidia separantur,
spans.english: Of the cities set apart to aid fugitives, three shall be beyond the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, for both the children of Israel and sojourners and foreigners, so that anyone who has shed blood unintentionally may flee to them.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 35:13 ("De ipsis autem urbibus, quæ ad fugitivorum subsidia separantur,"); English continues through Vg 35:14-15 ("three shall be beyond the Jordan ... may flee to them").

spans.latin: Quod si fortuitu, et absque odio
spans.english: But if by accident and without hatred or enmity he does any of these things, and this is established in the people's hearing, after the question between the striker and the blood relative has been examined, the innocent man shall be freed from the avenger's hand and returned by judgment to the city to which he fled. He shall remain there until the high priest, anointed with holy oil, dies.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 35:22 ("Quod si fortuitu, et absque odio"); English continues through Vg 35:23-25 ("or enmity he does any of these things ... anointed with holy oil, dies").

spans.latin: ne commisceatur possessio filiorum Israël de tribu in tribum. Omnes enim viri ducent uxores de tribu et cognatione sua :
spans.english: so that the possession of the children of Israel may not be mixed from tribe to tribe. For all men shall take wives from their own tribe and clan, and all women shall take husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain within the families, and the tribes may not be mixed with one another, but remain as they were separated by the Lord. The daughters of Zelophehad did as they had been commanded.
spans.reason: Latin shown is Vg 36:7 only (ends "de tribu et cognatione sua"); English continues through Vg 36:8-10 ("and all women shall take husbands ... did as they had been commanded").

spans.ref: Esther 1:1 (Vulgate 11:2) (card shown on 17 rows, to Esther 1:1r)
spans.latin: Anno secundo, regnante Artaxerxe maximo, prima die mensis Nisan, vidit somnium Mardochæus filius Jairi, filii Semei, filii Cis, de tribu Benjamin :
spans.english: In the second year of the reign of the great Artaxerxes, on the first day of the month Nisan, Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, saw a dream. He was a Jewish man who lived in the city of Susa, a great man and among the foremost in the royal court. He was one of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported from Jerusalem with Jeconiah king of Judah. This was his dream: voices, tumult, thunder, an earthquake, and turmoil appeared upon the earth. Behold, there were two great dragons, ready to fight against each other. At their cry all the nations were stirred up to fight against the nation of the just. That day was a day of darkness and peril, tribulation and distress, and great fear upon the earth. The nation of the just was troubled, fearing its calamities, and prepared for death. They cried out to God, and as they raised their voices, a little spring grew into a very great river and overflowed in abundant waters. Light and the sun arose, and the lowly were exalted and devoured the mighty. When Mordecai had seen this and risen from his bed, he pondered what God intended to do. He kept it fixed in his mind, wishing to know what the dream meant. At that time he was staying in the king's court with Bagatha and Thara, the king's eunuchs, who were the palace doorkeepers. When he understood their thoughts and examined their concerns more closely, he learned that they were attempting to lay hands on King Artaxerxes, and he reported the matter to the king. The king questioned both men and, when they confessed, ordered them led away to death. The king recorded what had happened in the records, and Mordecai too committed an account of the event to writing. The king commanded him to remain in the palace court and gave him gifts for his report. But Haman son of Hammedatha, the Bugaean, was held in very great honor before the king, and he wished to harm Mordecai and his people because of the king's two eunuchs who had been killed. And they plundered their goods, or possessions. This was the copy of the letter.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 11:2; the English runs on through Vg 11:3-12:6 and ends with a fragment of Jerome's note ("And they plundered their goods... This was the copy of the letter"), which is not scripture text.

spans.ref: Esther 3:13a (Vulgate 13:1) (card shown on 7 rows, to Esther 3:13g)
spans.latin: Rex maximus Artaxerxes ab India usque Æthiopiam, centum viginti septem provinciarum principibus et ducibus qui ejus imperio subjecti sunt, salutem.
spans.english: The great King Artaxerxes sends greetings to the princes and rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia who are subject to his rule. When I ruled over many nations and had subjected the whole world to my authority, I wished by no means to abuse the greatness of my power, but to govern my subjects with mercy and gentleness, so that, passing their lives quietly and without any terror, they might enjoy the peace desired by all mortals. When I asked my counselors how this might be accomplished, one who excelled the others in wisdom and loyalty, who was second after the king and named Haman, informed me that there was a people scattered throughout the whole world who used strange laws, acted contrary to the customs of every nation, despised kings' commands, and disrupted the concord of all nations by their dissension. When we learned this and saw that a single nation, rebellious against the whole human race, used perverse laws, opposed our commands, and disturbed the peace and concord of the provinces subject to us, we ordered that all whom Haman identifies, who is set over every province, second after the king, and whom we honor as a father, should be destroyed by their enemies with their wives and children, and that no one should pity them, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, in this present year, so that these wicked people, descending to the underworld in a single day, might restore to our empire the peace they had disturbed. Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 13:1 (the greeting); the English runs on through Vg 13:2-7 and ends with "Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him", a phrase from Jerome's note (= 4:17), not part of the letter.

spans.ref: Esther 4:17a (Vulgate 13:8) (card shown on 9 rows, to Esther 4:17i)
spans.latin: Mardochæus autem deprecatus est Dominum, memor omnium operum ejus,
spans.english: Mordecai prayed to the Lord, remembering all His works, and said: Lord, Lord, almighty King, all things are placed under Your authority, and no one can resist Your will if You decree the salvation of Israel. You made heaven and earth and everything contained within the circuit of heaven. You are Lord of all, and no one can resist Your majesty. You know everything, and You know that I did not refuse to pay homage to the most arrogant Haman out of pride, contempt, or any desire for glory. For I would gladly have been ready to kiss even his footprints for Israel's salvation. But I feared to transfer the honor of my God to a human being, or to worship anyone except my God. Now, Lord King, God of Abraham, have mercy on Your people, for our enemies wish to destroy us and wipe out Your inheritance. Do not despise Your portion, which You redeemed for Yourself from Egypt. Hear my prayer, be gracious to Your lot and Your measured inheritance, and turn our mourning into joy, so that we may live and praise Your name, Lord. Do not close the mouths of those who sing to You. All Israel too, with one mind and plea, cried out to the Lord, because certain death hung over them.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 13:8 ("Mardochæus autem deprecatus est Dominum, memor omnium operum ejus"); the English continues with the whole prayer and the people's cry, Vg 13:9-18.

spans.ref: Esther 4:17k (Vulgate 14:1) (card shown on 15 rows, to Esther 4:17z)
spans.latin: Esther quoque regina confugit ad Dominum, pavens periculum quod imminebat.
spans.english: Queen Esther also fled to the Lord, trembling at the danger that threatened. She put aside her royal garments and put on clothing suited to weeping and mourning. Instead of various ointments, she covered her head with ashes and dung and humbled her body with fasting. She filled all the places where she had formerly rejoiced with hair she had torn out. She prayed to the Lord God of Israel, saying: My Lord, You alone are our King; help me in my solitude, for I have no other helper besides You. My peril is in my hands. I have heard from my father that You, Lord, chose Israel from all the nations, and our fathers from all their ancestors of old, to possess an everlasting inheritance. You did for them as You had promised. We have sinned in Your sight, and therefore You have handed us over to our enemies, for we worshiped their gods. You are just, Lord. Now it is not enough for them to oppress us with the harshest slavery. Attributing the strength of their hands to the power of idols, they wish to change Your promises, destroy Your inheritance, close the mouths of those who praise You, and extinguish the glory of Your temple and altar, so as to open the mouths of the nations, praise the strength of idols, and proclaim a king of flesh forever. Do not hand Your scepter, Lord, to those who are nothing, lest they laugh at our ruin. Turn their plan back upon them, and destroy the one who has begun to rage against us. Remember, Lord, and show Yourself to us in our time of tribulation. Give me confidence, Lord, King of gods and of every power. Put well-ordered speech in my mouth before the lion, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, so that the enemy and all who agree with him may perish. Deliver us by Your hand and help me, who have no other help except You, Lord, who know all things. You know that I hate the glory of the wicked and detest the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner. You know my necessity: I abhor the sign of my pride and glory that is upon my head on the days of my public display. I detest it like a menstruating woman's cloth and do not wear it in my days of quiet. I have not eaten at Haman's table; the king's banquet has not pleased me, and I have not drunk the wine of libations. Your maidservant has never rejoiced, from the time I was brought here until this day, except in You, Lord, God of Abraham. God, mighty above all, hear the voice of those who have no other hope. Deliver us from the hand of the wicked and rescue me from my fear.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 14:1 ("Esther quoque regina confugit ad Dominum, pavens periculum quod imminebat"); the English continues with the whole of Esther's prayer, Vg 14:2-19.

spans.ref: Esther 5:1d–1f (Vulgate 5:1) (card shown on 5 rows, to Esther 5:2b)
spans.latin: Die autem tertio induta est Esther regalibus vestimentis, et stetit in atrio domus regiæ, quod erat interius, contra basilicam regis : at ille sedebat super solium suum in consistorio palatii contra ostium domus.
spans.english: On the third day Esther put on her royal garments and stood in the inner court of the royal house, opposite the king's hall. He was sitting on his throne in the palace's audience chamber, facing the house's entrance. When he saw Queen Esther standing there, she pleased his eyes, and he extended toward her the golden scepter he held in his hand. She approached and kissed the tip of his scepter. On the third day she laid aside the garments of her adornment and clothed herself in her glory. Resplendent in royal dress, after calling upon God, the Ruler and Savior of all, she took two maidservants with her. She leaned upon one, as though her luxurious upbringing and extreme delicacy prevented her from supporting her own body. The other maidservant followed her mistress, holding up the garments that flowed to the ground. Her face was suffused with a rosy color and her eyes were gracious and bright, but she concealed a sorrowful spirit, constricted by great fear. Passing through all the doors in turn, she stood before the king, where he sat upon his royal throne, dressed in royal garments and shining with gold and precious stones. His appearance was fearsome. When he raised his face and showed the fury of his heart with blazing eyes, the queen collapsed. Her color turned pale, and she rested her weary head upon her young maidservant. God changed the king's spirit to gentleness. Quickly and anxiously he sprang from his throne and held her in his arms until she came to herself, soothing her with these words: What is the matter, Esther? I am your brother; do not be afraid. You will not die, for this law was established for everyone, not for you. Come, then, and touch the scepter. When she remained silent, he took the golden scepter and placed it upon her neck, kissed her, and said: Why do you not speak to me? She answered: I saw you, my lord, like an angel of God, and my heart was troubled with fear of your glory. For you are very wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of grace. While she was speaking, she collapsed again and almost lost consciousness. The king was distressed, and all his servants comforted her.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 5:1; the English continues with Vg 5:2 (the sceptre extended and kissed) and then the whole Greek-addition account of Esther's approach to the king, Vg 15:4-19.

spans.ref: Esther 8:12a (Vulgate 16:1) (card shown on 21 rows, to Esther 8:12x)
spans.latin: Rex magnus Artaxerxes ab India usque Æthiopiam, centum viginti septem provinciarum ducibus ac principibus qui nostræ jussioni obediunt, salutem dicit.
spans.english: The great King Artaxerxes sends greetings to the rulers and princes of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia who obey our command. Many have abused the goodness of rulers and the honor bestowed upon them, turning to pride. They endeavor not only to oppress kings' subjects but, unable to bear the glory given them, plot against the very men who gave it. They are not content to withhold thanks for benefits and violate the obligations arising from the kindness shown them; they also suppose that they can escape the judgment of God, who sees everything. They have broken out into such madness that they attempt, through the underground workings of lies, to overthrow those who diligently fulfill their entrusted duties and do everything in a manner worthy of everyone's praise. With cunning deceit they mislead the ears of rulers, who are trusting and judge others by their own character. Both ancient histories and daily events prove how the evil suggestions of certain people corrupt kings' intentions. Therefore provision must be made for the peace of all the provinces. You must not suppose that, if we issue different commands, it comes from fickleness of mind. Rather, we give judgment according to the character and necessity of the times, as the welfare of the state requires. To make our meaning clearer to you: Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian in both spirit and nationality, foreign to Persian blood and staining our goodness with his cruelty, was received by us as a foreigner. He experienced such kindness from us that he was called our father and received homage from everyone, second after the king. He swelled to such a height of arrogance that he attempted to deprive us of both kingdom and life. For he sought the death of Mordecai, through whose loyalty and services we are alive, and of Esther, the partner of our royal power, together with her entire nation, through strange and unheard-of schemes. He intended, once they were killed, to plot against us in our isolation and transfer the Persian kingdom to the Macedonians. But we have found that the Jews, whom this worst of mortals had marked for death, are entirely without fault and, on the contrary, follow just laws. They are children of the Most High, the greatest and ever-living God, through whose kindness the kingdom was handed down to our fathers and to us and is preserved to this day. Therefore know that the letters he sent under our name are void. For this crime, both the plotter and his entire family hang on gibbets before the gates of this city, Susa. It is God, not we, who has repaid him what he deserved. Let this edict that we now send be posted in every city, so that the Jews may be permitted to follow their own laws. You must assist them, so that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar, they may kill those who had prepared to put them to death. For almighty God has changed this day of grief and mourning into joy for them. Therefore keep this day among your other festivals and celebrate it with every gladness, so that in the future too it may be known that all who faithfully obey the Persians receive a reward worthy of their loyalty, while those who plot against their kingdom perish for their crime. Let every province and city unwilling to share in this solemn festival perish by sword and fire and be so utterly destroyed that it remains forever inaccessible not only to people but even to beasts, as an example of contempt and disobedience.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 16:1 (the greeting, ending "salutem dicit"); the English continues with the whole of the king's letter, Vg 16:2-24.

spans.ref: Esther 10:3a (Vulgate 10:4) (card shown on 10 rows, to Esther 10:3k)
spans.latin: Dixitque Mardochæus : A Deo facta sunt ista.
spans.english: Mordecai said: These things have been done by God. I have remembered the dream I saw, which signified these very things, and none of them has failed. The little spring that grew into a river, changed into light and sun, and overflowed with abundant waters is Esther, whom the king took as his wife and wished to be queen. The two dragons are Haman and me. The nations that assembled are those who attempted to destroy the name of the Jews. My nation is Israel, which cried out to the Lord, and the Lord saved His people. He delivered us from every evil and performed great signs and wonders among the nations. He ordained that there be two lots, one for God's people and the other for all the nations. Both lots came before God for all the nations on the day appointed from that time. The Lord remembered His people and had mercy on His inheritance. These days shall be observed in the month Adar, on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of that month, with every care and with joy, the people assembled in a single gathering, throughout all succeeding generations of the people of Israel.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 10:4 ("Dixitque Mardochæus : A Deo facta sunt ista"); the English continues with the whole interpretation of the dream and the institution of the days, Vg 10:5-13.

spans.latin: In finem. Psalmus David.
spans.english: For the end. A psalm of David. In the Lord I trust. How can you say to my soul, “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow”?
spans.reason: Latin is the title only; the English adds "In the Lord I trust. How can you say to my soul, Flee to the mountain like a sparrow?" = Vg 10:2 "In Domino confido ... sicut passer", absent.

spans.ref: Psalms 12:3 (Vulgate 12:2)
spans.latin: quamdiu ponam consilia in anima mea ; dolorem in corde meo per diem ?
spans.english: How long will I lay plans within my soul, with sorrow in my heart through the day? How long will my enemy be exalted above me?
spans.reason: Latin ends at "dolorem in corde meo per diem"; the English adds "How long will my enemy be exalted above me?" = Vg 12:3 "Usquequo exaltabitur inimicus meus super me?", absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 21:31 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 21:32)
spans.latin: Et anima mea illi vivet ; et semen meum serviet ipsi.
spans.english: My soul will live for Him, and my descendants will serve Him. The coming generation will be announced to the Lord, and the heavens will proclaim His righteousness to a people yet to be born, whom the Lord has made.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "semen meum serviet ipsi" (v. 31). English adds all of v. 32 ("Annuntiabitur Domino generatio ventura; et annuntiabunt cæli justitiam ejus populo qui nascetur, quem fecit Dominus"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 24:3 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 24:4)
spans.latin: Neque irrideant me inimici mei : etenim universi qui sustinent te, non confundentur.
spans.english: and let my enemies not mock me, for all who wait for You will not be put to shame. Let all who act unjustly without cause be put to shame. Show me Your ways, Lord, and teach me Your paths.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "non confundentur" (v. 3). English adds v. 4 ("Confundantur omnes iniqua agentes supervacue. Vias tuas, Domine, demonstra mihi, et semitas tuas edoce me"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 48:10 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 48:11)
spans.latin: et vivet adhuc in finem.
spans.english: and will still live to the end. He will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying; the senseless and the fool will perish together. They will leave their riches to strangers,
spans.reason: Latin shown is only "et vivet adhuc in finem" (v. 10). English adds v. 11 ("Non videbit interitum, cum viderit sapientes morientes: simul insipiens et stultus peribunt. Et relinquent alienis divitias suas"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 52:1 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 52:2)
spans.latin: In finem, pro Maëleth intelligentiæ David. [Dixit insipiens in corde suo : Non est Deus.
spans.english: For the end, for Mahalath, for understanding, of David. The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupted and have become abominable in their iniquities; no one does good.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "Non est Deus" (v. 1). English adds v. 2 ("Corrupti sunt, et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus; non est qui faciat bonum"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 58:4 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 58:5)
spans.latin: Quia ecce ceperunt animam meam ; irruerunt in me fortes.
spans.english: For see, they have seized my soul; the mighty have rushed against me. It is neither my iniquity nor my sin, Lord; without iniquity I have run and kept straight.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "irruerunt in me fortes" (v. 4). English adds v. 5 ("Neque iniquitas mea, neque peccatum meum, Domine; sine iniquitate cucurri, et direxi"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 59:6 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 59:7)
spans.latin: Dedisti metuentibus te significationem, ut fugiant a facie arcus ; ut liberentur dilecti tui.
spans.english: You have given a sign to those who fear You, so that they may flee from the bow, so that Your beloved may be delivered. Save with Your right hand and hear me.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "ut liberentur dilecti tui". English adds the next clause ("salvum fac dextera tua, et exaudi me", Vg v. 7), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 61:12 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 61:13)
spans.latin: Semel locutus est Deus ; duo hæc audivi : quia potestas Dei est,
spans.english: Once God has spoken; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to You, Lord, for You will repay each one according to his works.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "quia potestas Dei est," (v. 12). English adds v. 13 ("et tibi, Domine, misericordia: quia tu reddes unicuique juxta opera sua"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 63:5 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 63:6)
spans.latin: ut sagittent in occultis immaculatum.
spans.english: to shoot the unstained man in hidden places. Suddenly they will shoot him and will not fear; they have confirmed an evil word among themselves. They have talked of hiding snares; they have said, “Who will see them?”
spans.reason: Latin shown is only "ut sagittent in occultis immaculatum" (v. 5). English adds v. 6 ("Subito sagittabunt eum, et non timebunt; firmaverunt sibi sermonem nequam. Narraverunt ut absconderent laqueos; dixerunt: Quis videbit eos?"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 71:1 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 71:2)

spans.english: A psalm concerning Solomon. God, give Your judgment to the king and Your righteousness to the king's son, to judge Your people with righteousness and Your poor with judgment.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only the title "Psalmus, in Salomonem" (v. 1). English adds v. 2 ("Deus, judicium tuum regi da, et justitiam tuam filio regis; judicare populum tuum in justitia, et pauperes tuos in judicio"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 73:5 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 73:6)

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "Quasi in silva lignorum securibus" (v. 5). English adds v. 6 ("exciderunt januas ejus in idipsum; in securi et ascia dejecerunt eam"), absent from the Latin.

spans.ref: Psalms 83:12 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 83:13)

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "gratiam et gloriam dabit Dominus"; the English runs on into Vg 83:13 ("Non privabit bonis eos qui ambulant in innocentia: Domine virtutum, beatus homo qui sperat in te"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 89:5 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 89:6)
spans.latin: quæ pro nihilo habentur, eorum anni erunt.
spans.english: things counted as nothing—such their years will be. In the morning let it pass like grass; in the morning let it bloom and pass; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only Vg 89:5 ("quæ pro nihilo habentur, eorum anni erunt"); the English runs on through Vg 89:6 ("Mane sicut herba transeat ... induret et arescat"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 90:4 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 90:5)
spans.latin: Scapulis suis obumbrabit tibi, et sub pennis ejus sperabis.

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "sub pennis ejus sperabis"; the English also gives Vg 90:5 ("Scuto circumdabit te veritas ejus: non timebis a timore nocturno"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 94:8 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 94:9)

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "nolite obdurare corda vestra"; the English runs on through Vg 94:9 ("sicut in exacerbatione ... probaverunt et viderunt opera mea"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 99:1 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 99:2)
spans.latin: Psalmus in confessione.
spans.english: A psalm of thanksgiving. Shout for joy to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter His presence with rejoicing.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only the title "Psalmus in confessione."; the English also gives Vg 99:2 ("Jubilate Deo, omnis terra; servite Domino in lætitia. Introite in conspectu ejus in exsultatione"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 108:1 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 108:2)
spans.latin: In finem. Psalmus David.
spans.english: For the end. A psalm of David. God, do not be silent about my praise, for the sinner's mouth and the deceitful mouth have opened against me.
spans.reason: Latin shown is only the title "In finem. Psalmus David."; the English also gives Vg 108:2 ("Deus, laudem meam ne tacueris, quia os peccatoris et os dolosi super me apertum est"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Psalms 108:16
spans.latin: pro eo quod non est recordatus facere misericordiam,
spans.english: because he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the needy and destitute person, the one pierced in heart, to put him to death.
spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "facere misericordiam,"; the English runs on into Vg 108:17 ("Et persecutus est hominem inopem et mendicum, et compunctum corde, mortificare"), whose Latin appears in no unit.

spans.ref: Psalms 110:6 (card shown on 2 rows, to Psalms 110:7)
spans.latin: Virtutem operum suorum annuntiabit populo suo,

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "annuntiabit populo suo,"; the English also gives Vg 110:7 ("ut det illis hæreditatem gentium. Opera manuum ejus veritas et judicium"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.latin: Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam :

spans.reason: Latin shown ends at "sed nomini tuo da gloriam :"; the English also gives the next verse ("super misericordia tua et veritate tua; nequando dicant gentes: Ubi est Deus eorum?"), whose Latin is not shown.

spans.ref: Song of Songs 7:1 (Vulgate 6:12) (card shown on 2 rows, to Song of Songs 7:2)
spans.latin: Revertere, revertere, Sulamitis ! revertere, revertere ut intueamur te.]
spans.english: [Chorus] Return, return, Shulammite! Return, return, that we may look upon you. [Bride] What will you see in the Shulammite, except the dances of the camps? [Chorus] How beautiful are your steps in sandals, prince's daughter! The joints of your thighs are like necklaces made by the hand of an artisan.
spans.reason: Latin shows only Vg 6:12 ('Revertere ... ut intueamur te'); English runs on through Vg 7:1 ('What will you see in the Shulammite ... hand of an artisan'), whose Latin is absent. Latin also ends with a stray ']'.

spans.ref: Acts 8:7
spans.latin: Multi enim eorum qui habebant spiritus immundos, clamantes voce magna exibant. Multi autem paralytici et claudi curati sunt.
spans.english: For many of them who had unclean spirits, crying with a loud voice, went out.
spans.reason: English stops short: "Multi autem paralytici et claudi curati sunt" is not rendered here; its English appears under 8:8.

spans.ref: Acts 8:8
spans.latin: Factum est ergo gaudium magnum in illa civitate.
spans.english: And many, taken with the palsy, and that were lame, were healed.
spans.reason: English renders the end of the previous Latin verse (paralytici et claudi curati sunt), not "Factum est ergo gaudium magnum in illa civitate", whose English is under 8:9.

spans.ref: Acts 8:9
spans.latin: Vir autem quidam nomine Simon, qui ante fuerat in civitate magus, seducens gentem Samariæ, dicens se esse aliquem magnum:
spans.english: There was therefore great joy in that city. Now there was a certain man named Simon who before had been a magician in that city, seducing the people of Samaria, giving out that he was some great one:
spans.reason: English begins with "There was therefore great joy in that city", which renders the Latin of 8:8 ("Factum est ergo gaudium magnum"), not this verse.

spans.ref: Acts 23:25
spans.latin: (Timuit enim ne forte raperent eum Judæi, et occiderent, et ipse postea calumniam sustineret, tamquam accepturus pecuniam.)
spans.english: (For he feared lest the Jews might take him away by force and kill him: and he should afterwards be slandered, as if he was to take money.) And he wrote a letter after this manner:
spans.reason: English ends with "And he wrote a letter after this manner:", which renders "Scribens epistolam continentem hæc" at the head of the next Latin verse (23:26), not anything in this verse.

spans.ref: Acts 23:26
spans.latin: Scribens epistolam continentem hæc: Claudius Lysias optimo præsidi Felici, salutem.
spans.english: Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor, Felix, greeting:
spans.reason: English stops short: "Scribens epistolam continentem hæc" (writing a letter containing this) is not rendered here; it is displayed under 23:25 instead.

spans.ref: 2 Corinthians 8:14
spans.latin: In præsenti tempore vestra abundantia illorum inopiam suppleat: ut et illorum abundantia vestræ inopiæ sit supplementum, ut fiat æqualitas, sicut scriptum est:
spans.english: In this present time let your abundance supply their want, that their abundance also may supply your want: that there may be an equality,
spans.reason: The Latin verse ends with 'sicut scriptum est:' but the English stops short; 'As it is written:' is printed at the head of the next unit (8:15).

spans.ref: 2 Corinthians 8:15
spans.latin: Qui multum, non abundavit: et qui modicum, non minoravit.
spans.english: As it is written: He that had much had nothing over; and he that had little had no want.
spans.reason: English opens with 'As it is written:', which renders 'sicut scriptum est:' at the end of the previous Latin verse (8:14), not anything in this Latin.
